# Audit: convex triangle-free unit-rhombus tilings are full two-axis grids

**Verdict: PASS for geometric Steps 1–4 of worker428.** Under the stated whole-hull tiling hypotheses there is no T-junction, track-end, track-crossing, boundary-subdivision, or extra-vertex exception. The argument below supplies the finite cell-complex and crosscut details explicitly.

This audit does not recheck the later finite grid deformation or its local-optimality consequence. It does not extend the result to nonconvex patches, rhombi filling only part of the hull, holes, or extra points outside the tiled region.

## Precise hypotheses and conclusion

Let `P` be a finite planar point set with pairwise distances at least one, and let `K=conv(P)` have nonempty interior. Suppose `K` is the union of nondegenerate closed rhombi of side length one with disjoint interiors. Every tile vertex belongs to `P`, and every point of `P` is a tile vertex. Suppose the **full** unit-distance graph of `P` has no triangle.

Then there are linearly independent unit vectors `u,v`, a point `p0`, and positive integers `M,N` such that

    P={p0+i*u+j*v : 0<=i<=M, 0<=j<=N, i,j integers}.

The tiling consists of precisely the `MN` elementary rhombi of this grid. The smaller angle between the two unoriented axes of `u,v` lies in `(pi/3,pi/2]`.

No stress, local optimality, global optimality, or central-symmetry premise is used for this classification.

## 1. The tiling is a finite edge-to-edge cell decomposition

It is finite: its vertices are drawn from the finite set `P`, so there are only finitely many possible four-vertex rhombi, and repeated copies with the same interior cannot occur in a tiling with disjoint interiors.

Distinct drawn unit segments cannot cross properly. At a putative crossing, choose on each segment its nearer endpoint. Each chosen endpoint is at distance at most one half from the crossing. The segments have different line directions, so the strict triangle inequality gives a distance strictly less than one between the two chosen, distinct points of `P`, a contradiction.

A tile vertex cannot lie strictly inside any tile edge, since that unit edge would put it at distance less than one from an endpoint. Partial collinear overlap of two distinct unit edges is likewise impossible: it would place an endpoint strictly inside the other edge. Consequently tile edges can meet only at common endpoints or as identical full edges. This rules out T-junctions and unrecorded boundary subdivisions.

The disjoint-interior tiling condition excludes any remaining nesting or vertex-in-interior intersection of different tiles. Each interior edge has exactly two incident tiles, one on each side: there can be at most one on either side because two rhombi sharing an edge and the same side overlap near its relative interior; the union being all of `K` requires both sides at an interior edge. A boundary edge has one incident tile. Thus these tiles form a finite edge-to-edge cell decomposition of the convex polygon `K`.

The tile-edge graph is connected. For example, a generic path between two tile interior points inside the convex disk `K` avoids the finitely many tile vertices and crosses shared edges; it gives an edge-adjacency chain of tiles. Every tile boundary is a connected graph, and boundaries of consecutive tiles share an edge. Hence all tile vertices lie in one tile-edge component.

## 2. A track for one axis is an embedded boundary-to-boundary crosscut

Fix an unoriented tile-edge axis `u`, choose a unit representative, and choose a perpendicular unit normal `n_u`. For every tile with two edges parallel to `u`, draw the segment joining the midpoints of those two opposite edges. Within that tile this segment is parallel to its other edge axis. Its scalar projection on `n_u` has a nonzero change, because the tile is nondegenerate.

Concatenate these segments at midpoints of shared `u`-edges. At an interior such midpoint exactly two segments meet; at a boundary midpoint exactly one does. The resulting finite track graph has vertex degrees two internally and one at its possible boundary ends.

Orient each segment toward increasing `n_u` projection. These orientations agree across every shared `u`-edge. Indeed, the two tiles are on opposite sides of its supporting line. The segment in the tile on the lower side approaches that edge while increasing the projection; the one in the tile on the upper side leaves it while increasing the projection.

It follows that every track is globally strictly increasing in the `n_u` coordinate. There can be no cyclic track or self-intersection, since either would repeat a projection value at two different parameters. A finite component cannot have a nonboundary end, so every track is a simple arc with two boundary endpoints. Its relative interior lies in `int(K)`: segments lie in tile interiors except at shared-edge midpoint joints, and reaching a boundary-edge midpoint terminates the track.

Every boundary segment parallel to `u` is on one of the two supporting lines

    x dot n_u = min_{y in K}(y dot n_u),
    x dot n_u = max_{y in K}(y dot n_u).

This uses convexity of `K`. A straight boundary edge is a supporting edge of a convex polygon; the only two outward normal directions perpendicular to `u` are `n_u` and `-n_u`.

Since a track's projection increases strictly, its endpoints cannot be on the same such line. Therefore each `u`-track joins the two opposite supporting sides of `K` parallel to `u`. In particular, both supporting sides have positive length and contain boundary unit edges of this axis, even if `u` was first observed on an interior tile edge.

All endpoints are midpoints of unit boundary edges, so they lie in the relative interiors of their geometric supporting sides, never at a polygon corner. Collinear unit subdivisions of a supporting side cause no difficulty.

## 3. Every two distinct axes occur together in a rhombus

Let `u,v` be different unoriented tile-edge axes. The preceding construction provides a `u`-track joining the two supporting sides parallel to `u`, and a `v`-track joining the two supporting sides parallel to `v`.

These four geometric sides occur in alternating order around the boundary. To see this, choose representatives whose direction angles differ by a number strictly between zero and `pi`. Around the boundary of a convex polygon, the oriented tangent directions occur in cyclic angular order. The four distinct directions parallel to these sides are thus ordered

    u, v, -u, -v

up to cyclic rotation and orientation reversal; other sides may occur between them. Equivalently, their four outward normal directions occur in alternating antipodal pairs. No geometric side can serve both axes because the axes differ.

Thus the endpoints of **any** chosen `u`-track and `v`-track alternate on the boundary of the topological disk `K`. The tracks are embedded crosscuts with relative interiors in `int(K)`. The Jordan crosscut separation property forces them to intersect.

An intersection cannot be on a tile edge. A `u`-track meets the tiling edges only at midpoints of `u`-edges; a `v`-track does so only at midpoints of `v`-edges. Since those are distinct axes, equality of such edge points would contradict the edge-to-edge planar decomposition. Nor can either track pass through a tile vertex. Hence an intersection lies in the interior of one tile. That tile supports segments of both track families and therefore has its edge axes exactly `u` and `v`.

Consequently,

    every pair of distinct tile-edge axes occurs in some tile.       (A)

The proof does not assume that any two tracks cross at most once, nor does it assume a prior zonogon representation or global row offsets. Only a forced intersection is needed. In a tile with axes `u,v`, the corresponding midpoint segments meet at the tile center.

## 4. Triangle-freeness leaves exactly two axes

Let `alpha` be a tile's smaller interior angle, so `0<alpha<=pi/2`. Its shorter diagonal has length `2sin(alpha/2)`. Since both endpoints are points of `P`, unit separation forces `alpha>=pi/3`.

If `alpha=pi/3`, that diagonal has length one. Its endpoints and the tile vertex between their two incident unit sides form a unit equilateral triangle. This triangle lies in the **full** unit-distance graph, whether or not its diagonal was chosen as a tile edge. The triangle-free hypothesis therefore makes the inequality strict:

    pi/3 < alpha <= pi/2.                             (B)

By (A), the smaller angular distance between every pair of distinct unoriented axes exceeds `pi/3`. Unoriented directions form a circle of circumference `pi`. Three distinct axes would have three successive cyclic gaps summing to `pi`; each gap would have to exceed `pi/3`, since the smaller distance between its endpoint axes exceeds `pi/3`. This is impossible. Hence there are at most two axes.

There is at least one nondegenerate rhombus, which uses two axes, so there are exactly two. Write them as unit vectors `u,v`, choosing the signs later as needed along adjacent boundary sides. Statement (B) is unchanged by either sign choice.

## 5. Two axes force the entire full rectangular grid

Every tile boundary segment, and hence every segment making up `partial K`, is parallel to `u` or `v`. A nondegenerate convex polygon with just these two unoriented edge directions has four geometric sides, allowing collinear unit subdivisions. Opposite sides are parallel, so `K` is a parallelogram.

Choose one corner `p0` and choose the signs of `u,v` along its two outgoing sides. Every constituent boundary segment has length one. Thus the adjacent side lengths are positive integers `M,N`, and

    K={p0+s*u+t*v : 0<=s<=M, 0<=t<=N}.

The tile-edge graph is connected by Section 1, and each of its edge vectors is in `{u,-u,v,-v}`. Therefore every tile vertex is

    p0+i*u+j*v

for integers `i,j`. Since `u,v` are independent, these coordinates are unambiguous. Containment in `K` gives `0<=i<=M` and `0<=j<=N`.

Apply the invertible affine map taking `p0+s*u+t*v` to `(s,t)`. It takes `K` to `[0,M] x [0,N]`, and every tile becomes an axis-aligned unit square with integer vertices. Such a square is one of the standard cells

    [i,i+1] x [j,j+1],  0<=i<M, 0<=j<N.

All these `MN` cells must be present: a point in the interior of a missing standard cell cannot lie in any other integer unit cell, contradicting that the tiles cover the entire rectangle. Conversely no cell can occur twice because interiors are disjoint. The union of their vertex sets is precisely every integer grid point of the rectangle.

Finally, the hypothesis that `P` is exactly the set of tile vertices gives

    P={p0+i*u+j*v : 0<=i<=M, 0<=j<=N, i,j integers}.

This proves the full geometric classification.

## Essential scope and attribution

The whole-hull convexity is essential at two exact steps: a boundary edge parallel to `u` must lie on a global supporting line, and the four supporting sides of two different axes must alternate. In a nonconvex patch, tracks can end at unrelated boundary pieces and their endpoints need not alternate. Filling only part of a convex hull, leaving holes, or adding points outside the tiled region is therefore not covered.

The use of the **full** unit graph in the triangle-free assumption is also essential at the equality angle `pi/3`; the tiling skeleton alone may omit the unit diagonal forming the triangle.

The underlying track argument is classical rhombus-tiling geometry. Browser worker428 supplied this elementary proof route and its application. This focused native audit independently checked only the geometric classification, adding the finite cell-complex, support-side, and crosscut details above. It makes no historical priority claim. No external classification theorem, computation, or proof of the full Erdős #99 conjecture is asserted.

# Focused audit: elementary stress connectivity in the central case

**Verdict: PASS.** The proposed simplification is valid. It removes the universal physical-stress PSD theorem and the general stress-connectivity theorem from the central-symmetry argument. It requires the exact surviving active-vector invariant, rather than preservation of active lengths alone. This note verifies only that simplification; it does not re-audit the full elimination or terminal classification.

## Precise lemma

Let the ORIGINAL planar unit-separated packing `P=(p_i)` be centrally symmetric about zero, have diameter `D>1`, and let `R=D/2`. Let `iota` be its central label involution. Consider any normalized nonnegative physical equilibrium stress supported on original unit edges and original diameter edges:

    sum_j mu_ij (p_i-p_j) = sum_j lambda_ij (p_i-p_j),
    sum_{diameter edges} lambda_ij = 1.

Then the graph of positive unit weights has exactly one nontrivial connected component, and this component contains every endpoint of every positive diameter edge. No stress PSD, maximal support, triangle-freeness, local optimality, or stress symmetry is needed for this lemma.

## 1. All original diameter edges are antipodal

Central symmetry gives `D=2 max_i |p_i|=2R`. If `|p_i-p_j|=D`, equality in

    |p_i-p_j| <= |p_i|+|p_j| <= 2R

forces `|p_i|=|p_j|=R` and `p_j=-p_i`. Thus the original diameter graph is a matching on the outer circle. Put `lambda_i` equal to the weight of the possible antipodal diameter edge incident to `i`, and zero if no such positively weighted edge exists. The equilibrium equation becomes

    sum_j mu_ij (p_i-p_j) = 2 lambda_i p_i.       (1)

Whenever `lambda_i>0`, the right side is nonzero because `|p_i|=R>0`. Such a vertex has a positive unit edge and therefore lies in a nontrivial positive-contact component. The possible label at the original center has `lambda_i=0`; its presence changes none of the following arguments.

## 2. Every nontrivial positive-contact component surrounds the origin

Let `A` be a nontrivial connected component of the graph consisting of positive-`mu` unit edges. There are no positive contact edges between `A` and its complement. Sum (1) over its vertices. Internal contact forces cancel in opposite pairs, giving

    sum_{i in A} lambda_i p_i = 0.                (2)

There is at least one positive `lambda_i` in `A`. Otherwise dot (1) with `p_i` and sum over `i in A`. Each internal unit edge contributes `mu_ij |p_i-p_j|^2=mu_ij>0` to the left, while the right is zero. This is impossible.

Writing

    S_A = {p_i : i in A and lambda_i>0},

we obtain from (2), after dividing by the positive total weight, that

    0 belongs to conv(S_A).                       (3)

Every point in `S_A` lies on the SAME outer circle `|x|=R`. In particular `S_A` has at least two points. All coefficients in its displayed barycentric representation are positive; hence zero lies in its relative interior. The latter observation is useful but is not needed for the planar argument below.

## 3. Disjoint plane components cannot have intersecting terminal hulls

The following elementary fact is used.

**Circle-terminal fact.** Suppose two disjoint, connected, finite polygonal graphs are drawn in a closed disk and their respective nonempty terminal sets `S_A,S_B` lie on its boundary circle, with the two sets disjoint. Then `conv(S_A)` and `conv(S_B)` are disjoint.

Here is a detailed proof sufficient for the application. If one terminal set has one point, that point cannot be in the convex hull of other, distinct circle points: the tangent support line exposes it strictly. For sets of at least two points, the same strict exposure shows that neither hull can contain a vertex of the other hull. If the hulls meet, they must therefore have two properly intersecting chords, one with endpoints in each terminal set. This includes the cases of segment hulls. A mere vertex-on-edge contact is impossible by strict exposure. Collinear overlap of two chords with disjoint endpoint sets is impossible, because a line meets a circle in at most two points. For two two-dimensional hulls, absence of containment and intersection imply that their boundaries cross; for a segment and a polygon, both segment endpoints lie outside the polygon, so intersection gives a crossing. Thus there exist `a,c in S_A` and `b,d in S_B` alternating around the boundary circle.

A simple graph path in the first component joins `a` to `c`; a simple path in the second joins `b` to `d`. Two disjoint paths in a disk cannot join alternating boundary points. One precise way to apply the Jordan curve theorem, accommodating extra boundary touches of the first path, is to perturb that simple finite polygonal path slightly into the open disk except at its endpoints. Since the two compact graph images are disjoint, their distance is positive, so this can be done without meeting the second graph. The resulting crosscut, together with either boundary arc from `a` to `c`, separates `b` from `d`. Any path joining the latter two must meet the crosscut, a contradiction. This proves the fact.

The actual positive-contact components satisfy its disjoint-drawing hypotheses. Straight unit-contact graphs of a unit-separated planar packing are plane. For example, if two distinct unit segments cross properly, select on each segment the endpoint closest to their intersection. Each selected endpoint is at most `1/2` from that intersection, and the strict triangle inequality between the two different segment directions makes their mutual distance strictly less than one. A vertex in the interior of a unit edge likewise violates separation. Distinct collinear overlapping unit segments also violate separation. Consequently different contact components have disjoint compact polygonal images. Their drawings lie in the radius-`R` disk because all their vertices, and hence all segments, lie in that convex disk.

If there were two nontrivial positive-contact components, their terminal hulls would both contain zero by (3), contradicting the circle-terminal fact. This also handles two antipodal two-terminal components: their diameter segments meet at zero, and the corresponding alternating-terminal paths are forbidden just as above. No exceptional case is created by a zero-stress center label or by a terminal hull meeting another at zero.

## 4. Existence and the location of all positive diameter endpoints

Normalization supplies a positive diameter edge. Its endpoint force in (1) is nonzero, so a nontrivial positive-contact component exists. Section 3 proves it is unique. Section 1 puts every positive diameter endpoint in a nontrivial component, and hence in that unique component. This proves the precise lemma.

## 5. Transfer from the nonsymmetric terminal packing to the original packing

In the finite-elimination application, write `x_i` for the terminal positions. Its physical stress is supported on surviving unit edges `F_*` and on original diameter edges `H`. By the active-vector induction,

    x_i-x_j = p_i-p_j

for EVERY edge on which either multiplier is supported. Substituting this identity term by term in every terminal equilibrium equation gives exactly the same equilibrium equation at the ORIGINAL positions `p_i`. Each supported unit edge has original length one; each supported diameter edge has original length `D`. Give all eliminated original unit edges weight zero. Nonnegativity and the normalization `sum lambda=1` are unchanged. Thus the preceding lemma applies on the original geometry.

The positive-support graphs are graphs on labels, so their connectedness and endpoint incidence conclusions transfer back immediately to the terminal configuration. In particular, no claim of global geometric central symmetry at the terminal packing is made or needed.

## Scope and attribution

This is the root-proposed elementary central-force/noncrossing simplification, independently checked here. It specializes the connectivity argument to an ORIGINAL centrally symmetric configuration and its exactly vector-preserving descendants. It does not establish universal stress connectivity for arbitrary original geometries, and it makes no historical priority claim or claim to settle Erdos Problem #99.

# Audit: four alternating boundary cable wrenches

Date: 28 October 2026. Root proposed this lemma and its component-cut application. Verdict: the sign, polar construction, positive uniqueness, and stated necessary cut condition are correct, with the explicit force-support hypotheses below. This note makes no priority claim or assertion about internal positive completion, regular-class invariance, physical diameter realization, or Erdős #99.

## 1. Setup and rotation convention

Let P=conv{p_0,...,p_{N-1}} be a strictly convex polygon whose vertices are listed COUNTERCLOCKWISE. Put the origin strictly inside P. Indices are cyclic. Define

    v_i = p_i-p_{i+1},
    zeta_i = cross(p_i,p_{i+1}),
    J(x,y) = (-y,x),
    q_i = J(v_i)/zeta_i.

Here J is counterclockwise rotation through 90 degrees. Since zero lies strictly to the left of each oriented boundary edge p_i p_{i+1}, zeta_i>0.

Clockwise rotation would give -q_i, rather than the stated polar vertex. It would preserve the affine-dependence conclusion by a common half-turn, but it is not the polar convention used here.

## 2. The q_i are exactly the polar vertices, in cyclic order

Use the polar

    P^circ = {q: q dot p <= 1 for every p in P}.

The identity (Jx) dot y=cross(x,y) gives

    q_i dot p_i = q_i dot p_{i+1} = 1.

The vector J(v_i) is the outward normal to the counterclockwise edge p_i p_{i+1}. Strict convexity puts every other p_j strictly on the inner side of that edge, so

    q_i dot p_j < 1 for j not in {i,i+1}.

Thus q_i is feasible for P^circ. The active normals p_i,p_{i+1} are linearly independent because their determinant is zeta_i>0, so their two active lines meet at a genuine polar vertex. Conversely, a polar vertex corresponds to an exposed edge of P, hence to one of these adjacent pairs. Therefore the q_i are exactly all polar vertices.

The outward normals to consecutive strictly convex edges rotate counterclockwise in the same boundary order. Since each q_i is a positive multiple of the corresponding normal, the q_i appear counterclockwise in their index order. They are in strictly convex position. In particular any four distinct indices a<b<c<d give a genuine convex quadrilateral A=q_a, B=q_b, C=q_c, D=q_d, and any three of them are noncollinear.

## 3. Force and torque signs

Use the proposed central-force convention: boundary edge i applies +mu_i v_i at p_i and -mu_i v_i at p_{i+1}. Reversing every cable's force convention changes both equations by global signs and does not affect their zero sets.

Suppose the chosen component contains the tail p_i but not the head p_{i+1}. Its crossing-edge force is +mu_i v_i and torque about zero is

    cross(p_i,mu_i v_i) = -mu_i zeta_i.

If instead it contains the head but not the tail, the force is -mu_i v_i and torque is

    cross(p_{i+1},-mu_i v_i) = +mu_i zeta_i.

For four transitions with signs s_a=s_c=+1, s_b=s_d=-1, zero total force and torque are therefore equivalent to

    sum_i s_i mu_i v_i = 0,
    sum_i s_i mu_i zeta_i = 0.

The latter equation is the negative of the actual total torque, so the proposed zero equation is correct. Choosing the complementary component reverses all signs and leaves the equations unchanged.

## 4. Positive affine dependence and uniqueness

Set w_i=mu_i zeta_i. Applying J to the force equation converts the wrench equations to

    w_a q_a + w_c q_c = w_b q_b + w_d q_d,
    w_a + w_c = w_b + w_d.

If the weights are positive, divide by their common mass W to obtain the intersection of the OPEN diagonals AC and BD. Those diagonals of a strictly convex quadrilateral meet at exactly one point in the interior of both. Its two positive barycentric representations determine all four ratios w_i/W, and hence all mu_i ratios. Conversely, that intersection supplies a strictly positive solution. Only the common scale W>0 is free.

Equivalently, the affine-coordinate matrix with columns (q_i^x,q_i^y,1) has rank three, so its kernel is one-dimensional, with alternating signs. Thus the entire nonzero nonnegative balanced-wrench cone is one strictly positive ray. If all four coefficients are allowed to be zero, the zero vector is an additional trivial solution, not a second ray.

An explicit formula makes the signs checkable. For ordered points define

    [X,Y,Z] = cross(Y-X,Z-X).

For A,B,C,D in counterclockwise convex order all four triple areas below are positive. Up to a common positive factor take

    w_a = [B,C,D],
    w_b = [A,C,D],
    w_c = [A,B,D],
    w_d = [A,B,C],
    mu_i = w_i/zeta_i.

The signed vector (w_a,-w_b,w_c,-w_d) is the cofactor nullvector of the affine-coordinate matrix. It satisfies both displayed equations and proves uniqueness directly.

## 5. Component-cut application

Consider a central-force framework on these N polygon vertices. Its cable edges are the boundary cycle, and ALL nonzero strut forces are supported on a forest with N-2 edges on these N vertices. A forest on N vertices with N-2 edges has exactly two graph components, say X and Y. The convex-thrackle condition is not needed for this counting or wrench argument.

Suppose the X/Y labels form exactly four nonempty blocks around the boundary. There are exactly four crossing boundary edges a,b,c,d in cyclic order, and their incidence signs alternate. At every vertex assume force equilibrium.

Sum force equilibrium over X. Each edge with both endpoints in X cancels pairwise, and every strut is internal to one forest component. Only the four crossing boundary cable forces remain. Sum the torques of those equilibrium equations about zero as well. Each internal central-force edge has zero total torque, because its two opposite forces lie on the line through its endpoints. Therefore the four remaining cable wrenches satisfy precisely the equations in Section 3.

Consequently, if the four cut coefficients are not all zero, they are all strictly positive and are fixed up to a single positive scale by the polygon and the four cut positions. In particular this necessary boundary ray is independent of the choice of internal strut trees, provided the same vertex partition and polygon are retained.

The support condition is essential: choosing an N-2-edge forest SUBSET of a larger strut support does not make the omitted strut forces cancel across its components. Likewise, additional intercomponent cable edges would contribute additional wrenches. Such configurations are outside the stated four-edge cut application.

## 6. What this does and does not establish

This proves a necessary, uniquely determined positive four-cable boundary balance. It also constructs such a boundary balance abstractly for any strictly convex polygon and four cut edges. It does not construct forces balancing the individual internal vertices; internal stress coefficients might fail to exist or might have the wrong sign. Changing the geometric polygon changes the computed ray. No regular-class invariance or realization by unit cables/equal diameter struts is inferred.

Attribution: Root supplied the proposed four-boundary-cut lemma and the application to two components of a covering convex-thrackle forest. This audit independently checked it using elementary polar duality, torque cancellation, and the affine circuit of four convexly ordered planar points, and supplied the explicit positive cofactor formula. No literature-priority assertion is made.

# Audit: covering convex-thrackle forests with any number of components

**Verdict: PASS.** For fixed cyclically ordered, distinctly labeled, strictly convex vertices, the formula is

    F_c(N) = [N/(2c)] 2^(N-2c) binom(N-c-1,c-1),

for `c>=2` and `N>=2c`, when there are exactly `c` components and NO isolated vertices. The monotone-chain step, uninterrupted FULL-label blocks, singleton cases, component ordering, and exact `2c` overcount all check. No finite computation is needed for the proof.

Here a convex thrackle means a straight-edge graph in which every two edges share an endpoint or cross properly. Crossings are not graph vertices. The theorem counts combinatorial candidates only; it imposes no common edge lengths, physical stresses, or actual-diameter constraints.

## 1. A component is an ordered grid-path tree

Fix a component `T` and select an edge `e` in another component; this is possible because `c>=2` and each component is nontrivial. Every edge of `T` properly crosses `e`, since it cannot share its endpoints. The two open arcs determined by the endpoints of `e` therefore partition the vertices of `T` into nonempty lists

    U=(u_1,...,u_a),  V=(v_1,...,v_b),

both read in the prescribed clockwise orientation. Every `T` edge joins the two lists.

Represent `u_p v_q` by `(p,q)`. With these SAME clockwise orders on the two arcs, distinct-endpoint edges with `p<r` cross precisely when `q<s`. Shared-endpoint edges have one coordinate equal. Thus all cells representing edges of `T` are pairwise comparable in product order and can be listed as one increasing chain.

The first cell is `(1,1)` and the last is `(a,b)`: every row and column occurs because every listed vertex is incident to an edge. Suppose two consecutive cells increased BOTH coordinates. Every earlier cell then uses only rows and columns below that gap, and every later cell uses only rows and columns above it. The two edge groups would have disjoint vertex sets, contradicting connectedness. Hence consecutive cells share a coordinate.

The tree has `m=a+b-1` edges. There are `m-1=a+b-2` transitions, each increasing exactly one coordinate by a positive integer. The total coordinate increase from `(1,1)` to `(a,b)` is also `a+b-2`. Every transition must therefore be a unit horizontal or vertical grid step. Conversely, such a grid path builds a tree: its first cell is an edge, and each subsequent step adds a new vertex by one new edge. It spans every row and column and all pairs of edges meet.

Thus the component choices, for fixed ordered `U,V`, number

    binom(a+b-2,a-1).                                (1)

This includes `a=1` or `b=1`, where the component is a star and the grid path is unique, and `a=b=1`, where it is a single edge.

## 2. The two classes are uninterrupted in the FULL cyclic order

The grid path shows that consecutive `U` vertices `u_p,u_(p+1)` share some `V` neighbor `v`. If a label `x` occurred strictly between them on their common external-chord arc, then `x` could belong to neither `U` nor `V`. It would belong to another component. The no-isolates assumption supplies an edge `xz`.

The cyclic order is

    u_p, x, u_(p+1), v.

To cross `u_p v`, the endpoint `z` must lie in the open arc `(v,u_p)`. To cross `u_(p+1) v`, it must lie in the disjoint open arc `(u_(p+1),v)`. These are incompatible. Since the components have disjoint vertex sets, shared-endpoint exceptions cannot occur. Therefore no FULL-circle label intervenes between consecutive `U` vertices. The identical argument applies to `V`.

If a class has one vertex, it is already a singleton consecutive block; no additional argument is required. The connected tree's bipartition is unique up to swapping its two classes, so these two blocks are intrinsic, independent of the external chord chosen for the proof.

The no-isolates condition is essential here: an isolated label would have no edge `xz` and could interrupt a class block.

## 3. The global block order and its converse

Every component now has two nonempty FULL-circle blocks. Select one edge from each component. The `c` selected chords have disjoint endpoints and cross pairwise. For pairwise crossing chords, the cyclic component-name sequence on their endpoints is

    1,2,...,c,1,2,...,c,

after choosing a start and naming components. Indeed, fixing the first chord puts one endpoint of every other chord in each complementary arc; their clockwise orders on those arcs must agree for pairwise crossing.

Each selected endpoint lies in its component's intrinsic uninterrupted block. Consequently the blocks themselves have order

    A_1,...,A_c,B_1,...,B_c,                          (2)

where component `i` connects `A_i` to `B_i`. Every vertex belongs to exactly one such block, so there are exactly `2c` blocks. In particular no extra blocks are hidden by singleton classes.

Conversely, choose any positive sizes `a_i=|A_i|`, `b_i=|B_i|` and place the blocks in (2). Choose any path counted by (1) in each opposite-block pair. Within a component its edges meet by Section 1. Between components `i<j`, the endpoint blocks occur as `A_i,A_j,B_i,B_j`, so EVERY pair of edges from those two components crosses properly. This constructs exactly the required forest and proves necessity and sufficiency of the decomposition.

## 4. Count and exact multiplicity

Root a specification at the first label of its starting block, giving `N` possible circular positions. The fixed clockwise orientation then names the first `c` blocks `A_1,...,A_c` and the remaining ones `B_1,...,B_c`; no independent permutation of components is added.

For fixed ordered component sizes `n_i=a_i+b_i>=2`, summing (1) over its positive splits gives

    sum_{a_i=1}^{n_i-1} binom(n_i-2,a_i-1)=2^(n_i-2).

Multiplying over components gives `2^(N-2c)`. The number of ordered size compositions `sum_i n_i=N`, `n_i>=2`, is

    binom(N-c-1,c-1).

Hence the number of rooted specifications is

    N 2^(N-2c) binom(N-c-1,c-1).

Each unrooted labeled forest has EXACTLY `2c` such specifications, one for each intrinsic block boundary. Once the starting boundary is chosen, the component names, which class is called `A` versus `B`, the sizes, and the grid paths are all determined. No additional factor of `c!`, `2^c`, or two for reversal is appropriate. Clockwise orientation was fixed throughout; the forest is not being quotiented by geometric reflection. Rotational symmetry also does not reduce the multiplicity, since different starting boundaries have different first LABELS, even if their size/path patterns repeat.

Dividing by `2c` proves the formula.

As endpoint checks, `N=2c` gives one forest, the unique pairwise crossing perfect matching; `c=2` gives the previously obtained `N(N-3)2^(N-6)`. The case `c=1` is outside the proof because there is no external chord.

## Scope and attribution

Root proposed the formula. Worker431 supplied this self-contained arbitrary-`c` structural proof, independently verified here. Its reported finite enumeration was not rerun in this audit and is not needed for acceptance of the combinatorial proof. No historical priority, stress-sign classification, common-diameter realization, or resolution of Erdos99 is claimed.

# Audit: a square-root number of original positive diameter branch vertices

**Verdict: PASS, using the newly checked selected-core linear branching budget and the OLD additive corner bound in verified notes §44.** The transfer to an original joint-maximal positive diameter support is valid. The degree excess is monotone under adding edges even when new endpoints appear. No mixed-rank assertion at the original configuration is needed.

This is a new combination of existing inputs, not a new proof of §44 and not a solution of Erdős Problem #99.

## 1. Statement and imported inputs

Let `P` be a triangle-free GLOBAL minimum-diameter planar unit-separated packing, of diameter `D>=9`. Let `G=G(P)` be the positive diameter-edge support of a JOINT maximal-support normalized physical stress. Define

    S_G={v: d_G(v)>0},
    k_G=|E(G)|,
    h_G=|S_G|,
    eta_G=2k_G-h_G,
    B_G=|{v: d_G(v)>=2}|.

Suppose its actual convex-hull area deficit satisfies

    T=pi D^2/4-area(conv(P)) <= C D,

with `C>0` and `D>=8C/pi`. Then

    B_G >= (D-4)^(3/2)
           / [5^(3/2) sqrt(512 pi^2 C) D].                    (1)

Thus `B_G=Omega(sqrt(D))` for a fixed uniform area constant `C`. The same lower bound holds for the number of vertices of degree at least two in the original FULL actual diameter graph, which contains `G`.

The imported inputs are:

1. Joint-maximal finite weak-row release followed by local lexicographic selection retains every point label and the diameter `D`, and produces a selected full actual diameter graph `H_*` satisfying `E(H_*) subset E(G(P))`.
2. At this selected point, the accepted normal form gives `k_*>=ceil(D)` and the classical diameter-graph bound gives `h_*>=k_*`.
3. The new selected-core track-counting result, checked in `audit-linear-diameter-branching-budget.md`, gives

       eta_*=2k_*-h_* >= (h_*-4)/5.

4. OLD verified notes §§29,44 give, at the ORIGINAL packing and its ORIGINAL global convex hull, the degree/normal-cone bound and additive corner estimate

       d_actual(v)-1 <= D omega_v,
       sum over hull corners v of omega_v^3 <= 512 pi^2 C / D.

These are accepted proof inputs. This audit checks their combination, its graph monotonicity, and the original-point scope. It does not duplicate the Fourier proof of the additive corner estimate.

## 2. Degree excess is monotone under edge inclusion

For any finite simple graph `J`, count only its positive-degree endpoints in `h(J)`. Then

    eta(J)=2|E(J)|-h(J)
          =sum_{v:d_J(v)>0}(d_J(v)-1)
          =sum_v max(d_J(v)-1,0).                            (2)

The final sum may be over the entire fixed label set, including graph isolates. The positive-part convention is important; summing `(d_J(v)-1)` over isolates without it would be incorrect.

Adding a new edge changes `eta` by:

- `2`, if both its endpoints already have positive degree;
- `1`, if exactly one endpoint already has positive degree;
- `0`, if both endpoints were isolated.

In every case it is nondecreasing. This also follows immediately from the last expression in (2), since each vertex degree is nondecreasing under edge addition.

The accepted label-preserving inclusion `H_* subset G(P)` therefore yields

    eta_G >= eta_*
          >= (h_*-4)/5
          >= (ceil(D)-4)/5
          >= (D-4)/5.                                         (3)

Only the selected graph uses the mixed-rank/normal-form conclusions. This transfer is combinatorial: it does not require the selected coordinates, hull, normal cones, edge vectors, or individual stress weights to agree with those of the original packing.

In particular, (3) does NOT claim `eta_G>=(h_G-4)/5`. That stronger original-endpoint formulation would not follow just from monotonicity, since adding a disjoint matching edge increases `h_G` by two while leaving `eta_G` unchanged. The correct transferred lower bound is in terms of the unchanged diameter `D`.

## 3. Apply the old corner estimate at the original geometry

For every label put

    e_v=max(d_G(v)-1,0).

If `e_v>0`, the vertex is an actual-diameter endpoint of the ORIGINAL packing and hence a strictly exposed corner of its ORIGINAL global convex hull. Its degree in the positive support is at most its degree in the full actual diameter graph. Therefore the degree/normal-cone bound gives

    0<=e_v=d_G(v)-1<=d_actual(v)-1<=D omega_v.

Summing cubes over the subset where `e_v>0`, then enlarging to all hull corners, gives

    sum_v e_v^3
       <= D^3 sum_hull omega_v^3
       <= 512 pi^2 C D^2.                                   (4)

It is not necessary for `G` to contain every actual diameter edge. A degree-one vertex contributes zero to this moment; an isolated label also contributes zero by definition. No assertion that a zero-stress hull vertex is loaded is used.

The area condition and normal cones are those of the ORIGINAL global packing. There is consequently no need to transport area control or original hull geometry through finite release.

## 4. Hölder gives the branch-vertex count

Exactly `B_G` terms `e_v` are positive, and by (2) their sum is `eta_G`. Hölder's inequality gives

    eta_G = sum_{e_v>0} e_v
          <= B_G^(2/3) (sum_v e_v^3)^(1/3).

Since `D>=9`, (3) is positive, so `B_G>0`. Cubing and using (4),

    eta_G^3 <= B_G^2 * 512 pi^2 C D^2.

Taking square roots and substituting (3) proves (1). If desired, the integer lower bound is the ceiling of its displayed right side.

For example, since `D-4>=D/2` when `D>=8`, the simpler uniform consequence is

    B_G >= sqrt(D) / [10^(3/2) sqrt(512 pi^2 C)].                (5)

Adding the remaining actual diameter edges cannot lower any vertex degree, so `B_fullH>=B_G`; (1) and (5) also hold for the full actual graph.

## 5. An explicit global area constant from Oler and nonnegative reserve

Write `a0=sqrt(3)/2`, `rho=pi/(2sqrt(3))`, `L=per(conv(P))`, and `g=n-1-rho D^2`. Whenever the previously established global population reserve gives `g>=0`, the classical convex Oler inequality implies

    n <= area(conv(P))/a0 + L/2 + 1,

and hence

    T <= a0 L/2-a0 g <= a0 pi D/2
      = (pi sqrt(3)/4) D.

Here `L<=pi D` is Cauchy's perimeter bound. Thus one may take

    C=pi sqrt(3)/4.

Its threshold `8C/pi=2sqrt(3)` is already implied by `D>=9`. Nonnegativity of the global reserve is available, in particular, in the established sufficiently-large-diameter regime; no new packing construction is used by this corollary.

With this choice, (1) becomes

    B_G >= (D-4)^(3/2)
           / [40 sqrt(10) pi^(3/2) 3^(1/4) D].               (6)

This coefficient is a sufficient explicit constant, not an optimality claim.

# Audit: Grünbaum reference stress and exact unit-boundary exclusion

**Verdict: the coefficients, PSD argument, and exclusion are valid for every odd \(N\ge7\), including composite \(N\).** No equality-case uniqueness theorem is needed. The exclusion also has a short independent geometric proof given below.

## 1. Exact coefficients and equilibrium

Put \(x=\pi/N\), \(R=(2\sin x)^{-1}\), and \(p_j=R(\cos 2jx,\sin 2jx)\). Let
\[
H=\{(0,j):2\le j\le N-2\}\cup\{(1,N-1)\}.
\]
Use worker336's unnormalized coefficients:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mu_0=\mu_{N-1}&=\frac{\sin3x}{\sin x},\\
\mu_j&=\frac{\sin x\sin2x}{\sin jx\sin((j+1)x)}
 &&(1\le j\le N-2),\\
\lambda_j&=\frac{\mu_{j-1}\sin x\sin2x}{\sin jx\sin((j+1)x)}
 &&(2\le j\le N-2),\\
\lambda_*&=1.
\end{aligned}
\]
All are strictly positive. At \(j\in I=\{2,\ldots,N-2\}\), the vector equilibrium is equivalent to
\[
\mu_{j-1}\sin((j-1)x)=\mu_j\sin((j+1)x),\qquad
\lambda_j\sin jx
=\sin x\bigl(\mu_{j-1}\cos((j-1)x)-\mu_j\cos((j+1)x)\bigr).
\]
The first follows from the formula for \(\mu\); substitution into the second gives exactly the displayed \(\lambda_j\). At vertex \(1\), the required identity is
\[
\frac{\sin3x}{\sin x}e^{ix}-e^{3ix}=2\cos x,
\]
which proves equilibrium because \(\mu_1=\lambda_*=1\). Reflection handles \(N-1\), and summing the other equilibrium equations handles \(0\).

Divide every coefficient by \(L=1+\sum_{j=2}^{N-2}\lambda_j\). Then \(\sum_H\lambda=1\), with positivity and equilibrium unchanged.

## 2. PSD and exact scalar nullity

Let \(\Omega=L_{\partial}(\mu)-L_H(\lambda)\), \(B=\{0,1,N-1\}\), and \(A=\Omega_{II}\). The affine height
\[
z_j=R\cos2x-(p_j)_x
\]
is zero on \(B\setminus\{0\}\), strictly positive on \(I\), and negative at \(0\). Equilibrium gives \(\Omega z=0\). Since \(\Omega_{i0}=\lambda_i\),
\[
Az_I=-z_0\lambda_I>0.
\]
The only off-diagonal entries of \(A\) are the nonpositive boundary-chain entries. For any \(w_i=z_i y_i\),
\[
w^\top Aw
=\sum_i z_i(Az)_i y_i^2
 +\sum_{i<j}(-A_{ij})z_i z_j(y_i-y_j)^2.
\]
The first coefficients are strictly positive, so \(A\) is positive definite.

The three affine vectors \(\mathbf1,p_x,p_y\) lie in \(\ker\Omega\). Their restrictions to \(B\) are independent because the three reference points are noncollinear. Therefore the Schur complement of \(A\) annihilates a basis of \(\mathbb R^3\) and is zero. Block congruence now proves
\[
\Omega\succeq0,\qquad
\ker\Omega=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf1,p_x,p_y\}.
\]

## 3. Energy exclusion for a target polygon

Let \(q_0,\ldots,q_{N-1}\) be a convex polygon in this cyclic order, with every boundary edge exactly \(1\), and suppose every edge of \(H\) is an actual diameter pair of common length \(D\). PSD gives
\[
0\le\operatorname{tr}(Q^\top\Omega Q)=\sum_{\partial}\mu-D^2.
\]
Reference equilibrium and unit reference sides give
\[
\sum_{\partial}\mu=\sum_H\lambda_e|p_i-p_j|^2.
\]
For odd \(N\), the regular reference diameter is
\[
D_{\rm reg}=\frac1{2\sin(\pi/(2N))}.
\]
Every reference chord has length at most \(D_{\rm reg}\). For \(N\ge7\), chord \((0,2)\) is strictly shorter and has positive weight. Hence
\[
\sum_{\partial}\mu<D_{\rm reg}^2.
\]
On the other hand, Reinhardt's perimeter inequality and target perimeter \(N\) give \(D\ge D_{\rm reg}\). Thus
\[
0\le\operatorname{tr}(Q^\top\Omega Q)
<D_{\rm reg}^2-D^2\le0,
\]
a contradiction.

This requires exact unit boundary lengths. Boundary lengths merely at least \(1\) do not give the same fixed-energy comparison. Full unit separation of nonadjacent target vertices is unnecessary for this argument.

## 4. Short independent exclusion

The target assumptions themselves give
\[
D=|q_1-q_{N-1}|
\le |q_1-q_0|+|q_0-q_{N-1}|=2.
\]
Every convex planar body's perimeter is at most \(\pi\) times its diameter. Therefore
\[
N=\operatorname{Per}(Q)\le\pi D\le2\pi<7\le N,
\]
already a contradiction for the requested odd \(N\ge7\).

The reference coefficients are those supplied by worker336; the PSD and energy calculations above independently verify the proposed root synthesis.

# Independent audit: the fully diameter-covered unit heptagon

## Verdict and exact scope

The claim passes. Let p_0,...,p_6 be, in counterclockwise order, a strictly convex heptagon with all consecutive sides of length one. Assume the supplied classical lower bound

D >= Dreg = 1+2 cos(2 pi/7).

If its FULL actual diameter graph covers all seven vertices and has at least five edges, the heptagon is regular. Its full actual diameter graph then has seven edges. In particular, a fully covering five- or six-edge actual diameter forest is impossible.

The worker's short proof omitted several branch justifications. They can all be supplied; a complete exact argument follows. No numerical acceptance is used. The classical lower bound above is the only imported geometric premise.

## 1. Exact preliminary facts

Put tau=2 pi/7 and X=cos(tau). The seventh-root identity gives

p(X)=0,   p(x)=8x^3+4x^2-4x-1.

Also X>1/2, and p is strictly increasing on (1/2,1), since

p'(x)=24x^2+8x-4>0 there.

For eta=(sqrt(5)-1)/2, direct substitution gives

p(eta)=4 sqrt(5)-9<0.

Thus X>eta>3/5. In particular

Dreg=1+2X>sqrt(5)>2,
1/(16 X^3)<1/3.

Every diameter pair must therefore have cyclic boundary separation three: separation one or two gives distance at most two. The only candidate diameter edges are

e_i={p_i,p_(i+3)},   i modulo 7.

Write u_i=p_(i+1)-p_i and let t_i be the exterior turn from u_(i-1) to u_i. Strict convexity gives

0<t_i<pi,   sum_i t_i=2 pi.

For positive turns x,y define

Q(x,y)=3+2 cos x+2 cos y+2 cos(x+y).

This is the squared length of three consecutive unit edges whose two intervening turns are x,y. Hence

|e_i|^2=Q(t_(i+1),t_(i+2)).

### Consecutive equal chords: the omitted branch is impossible

For x,y,z in (0,pi),

Q(x,y)-Q(y,z)
 =4 cos(y/2)[cos(x+y/2)-cos(z+y/2)].

If two consecutive three-edge chords have equal length, the positive factor cos(y/2) can be cancelled. Equality of the cosines gives either x=z, or x+y+z=2 pi times an integer. Here x,y,z are three of the seven positive turns, so

0<x+y+z<2 pi.

The latter branch is impossible. Consequently

|e_i|=|e_(i+1)| implies t_(i+1)=t_(i+3).

### A bound on the two turns of every diameter chord

If x+y>=pi, then cos x+cos y<=0 and Q(x,y)<=5. Thus Q(x,y)>5 implies x+y<pi. For 0<s<pi put

M(s)=(1+2 cos(s/2))^2.

The identity for cos x+cos y gives

Q(x,y)<=M(x+y),

with equality exactly when x=y. M is strictly decreasing on (0,pi). Since

D^2>=Dreg^2=M(2 tau)>5,

every diameter chord with intervening turns x,y satisfies

x+y<=2 tau.

## 2. Six or seven diameter edges

If at least six candidate edges occur, relabel so e_1,...,e_6 are all diameters. Applying the consecutive-chord identity gives

(t_0,...,t_6)=(b,a,a,b,a,b,a),
4a+3b=2 pi.

Rotate so u_0=1. With z=exp(i a/3), w=exp(2 pi i/3), the edge vectors are

1, z^3, z^6, w z^2, w z^5, w^2 z, w^2 z^4.

These are exactly the powers of q=w^2 z with exponents 0,...,6, in a different order. Closure therefore gives

1+q+...+q^6=0,

so q is a nontrivial seventh root of unity. Positivity gives 0<a<pi/2, hence the displayed argument of q lies in (4 pi/3,3 pi/2). The only seventh-root argument there is 10 pi/7. Therefore a=tau, and then b=tau. The heptagon is regular.

## 3. Exactly five diameter edges: the two missing-edge types

The seven candidates form the star cycle C_7. To cover all vertices after deleting two edges, the missing edges cannot share an endpoint. Candidate edges e_i and e_j share an endpoint precisely when j-i is 3 or 4 modulo 7. Up to polygon dihedral symmetry, the missing pair is therefore either {e_0,e_1} or {e_0,e_2}.

### Case A: missing e_0,e_1

Consecutive equalities give

(t_0,...,t_6)=(b,a,c,b,a,b,a),
3a+3b+c=2 pi.

Put s=a+b and v=a-b. Direct summation of the seven edge vectors, using u_0=1 and c=2 pi-3s, gives the exact closure equation

0=exp(-i s)[1+2 cos s+4 cos s cos(s/2) exp(i v/2)].

Here 0<s<2 pi/3 and |v|<s. If cos s=0, the bracket equals 1, impossible. Otherwise its imaginary part gives sin(v/2)=0, hence v=0. Thus a=b and 0<a<pi/3.

The real equation becomes p(cos a)=0. Since cos a lies in (1/2,1), strict monotonicity of p and p(cos tau)=0 force a=tau. Then b=c=tau.

### Case B: missing e_0,e_2

Consecutive equalities give

(t_0,...,t_6)=(b,a,c,d,a,b,a),
3a+2b+c+d=2 pi.

Put s=a+b. The present diameter edges yield

Q(a,b)=Q(c,d)=D^2,   s<=2 tau.

Summing edge vectors and using c+d=2 pi-a-2s gives

0=exp(-i s)(1+2 cos s)(1+exp(i a))+exp(i(a+c)).

Since 0<a<s<=2 tau<2 pi/3, both 1+2 cos s and cos(a/2) are positive. Moduli give

2 cos(a/2)(1+2 cos s)=1.                 (B1)

The phase difference is a/2+c+s. It lies strictly between 0 and 2 pi, so the opposite-phase condition has the unique possibility

c=pi-s-a/2.

The turn sum then gives d=c. There is no additional phase branch.

The regular values (a,s)=(tau,2 tau) satisfy (B1). Because s<=2 tau and 1+2 cos s decreases with s, (B1) implies a>=tau. Also a<s<2 pi/3 makes cos(a/2)>1/2; (B1) then implies s>pi/2.

For fixed a, (B1) has a unique s in (0,pi). On its branch between the regular point and the candidate point,

ds/da=-sin(a/2)/(8 cos(a/2)^2 sin s).

Throughout this interval, pi/2<s<=2 tau and a<2 tau. Therefore

0<-ds/da
 <= sin(tau)/(8 cos(tau)^2 sin(2 tau))
 =1/(16 cos(tau)^3)
 <1/3.

This branch really connects the two points: solving (B1) for cos s gives a continuous unique s(a), decreasing as a increases; between the endpoints it remains in (pi/2,2 tau]. Thus integration of 1+3 ds/da>0 gives

3s+a >= 7 tau=2 pi,

with equality only at a=tau.

On the other hand Q(c,c)=D^2>5 implies 2c<pi. Thus both arguments below are in the interval on which M is strictly decreasing, and

M(2c)=Q(c,c)=Q(a,b)<=M(s)

implies 2c>=s. Substituting c=pi-s-a/2 gives

3s+a<=2 pi.

Both inequalities force a=tau and s=2 tau. Hence b=c=d=tau. The polygon is regular.

## 4. Checked conclusion and limitations

The hypotheses force regularity in every case. In the regular unit heptagon all seven three-step chords are diameters, while one- and two-step pairs are shorter. Thus the FULL actual diameter graph has exactly seven edges, not five or six.

The potentially delicate points are all resolved: the extra cosine branch, the exact comparison Dreg^2>5, phase uniqueness, connectedness of the modulus branch, the strict derivative bound, and the domain 2c<pi needed for the final use of M.

The theorem concerns the full actual diameter graph on the seven polygon vertices. It does not alone exclude an arbitrarily chosen five-edge positive-stress subgraph of a larger actual diameter graph, and it supplies no conclusion for higher odd orders or for merely approximate unit sides.

# Audit: hull symmetry from isodiametric area deficit

**Verdict: the two analytic inequalities, the sharp RMS example, and all three regular-odd-rim constants PASS.** The phrase "best reflected-vertex pairing error" in worker414 should be replaced by the precise statement "nearest reflected-label error about center zero." That computation alone is not an involution statement. A cyclic bijection does attain that error in the regular polygon, but it is not an involution. For an odd label set an involution has a fixed label, giving a much larger obstruction, as explained in Section 6 below.

This audit does not claim any new conclusion for arbitrary globally minimizing unit packings.

## 1. Fourier setup, including nonsmooth hulls

Let `K` be a compact convex planar body of diameter `D>0`, area `A`, support function `h(theta)`, and Steiner point `c`. Put `R=D/2` and

    eta=pi R^2-A.

Write the real Fourier expansion with the following normalization:

    h(theta)=a_0+sum_{j>=1}(a_j cos(j theta)+b_j sin(j theta)).

The support function is Lipschitz on the circle, so it belongs to `H^1`. The Steiner point is `c=(a_1,b_1)`. Cauchy's perimeter identity and the width bound give

    2pi a_0=per(K)=integral_0^pi width_K(theta) dtheta <= pi D,

so `0<=a_0<=R`. The support-function area identity and Parseval give

    A=(1/2)integral_0^{2pi}(h^2-h'^2)
     =pi a_0^2-(pi/2)sum_{j>=2}(j^2-1)(a_j^2+b_j^2).

These formulas do apply to polygons. One precise justification is to convolve `h` with smooth nonnegative approximate-identity kernels on the rotation group, and add a vanishing positive constant. Such functions are support functions of Minkowski averages of rotations of `K`, plus a small disk; their smooth curvature radii are positive. They converge to `h` uniformly and in `H^1`. Area is continuous under Hausdorff convergence of convex bodies, so the smooth area identity passes to the displayed `H^1` identity. Parseval applies to both `h` and its weak derivative. Degenerate segments can also be obtained as a limit if desired.

Consequently

    eta=pi(R^2-a_0^2)
         +(pi/2)sum_{j>=2}(j^2-1)(a_j^2+b_j^2).

Every term is nonnegative. Define

    S=sum_{j>=3, j odd}(j^2-1)(a_j^2+b_j^2).

Then

    S<=2eta/pi.                                      (1)

## 2. Hausdorff reflection defect at the Steiner point

Translate by `-c`, removing the first Fourier harmonics. Let

    f(theta)=sum_{j>=3, j odd}(a_j cos(j theta)+b_j sin(j theta)).

The exact support-function characterization of Hausdorff distance gives

    delta=d_H(K,2c-K)=2||f||_infinity.

Weighted Cauchy--Schwarz, at any fixed angle, gives

    |f(theta)|^2
      <=S sum_{j>=3, j odd}1/(j^2-1)=S/4,

because

    sum_{m>=1}1/[(2m+1)^2-1]
      =(1/4)sum_{m>=1}(1/m-1/(m+1))=1/4.

There is no missing factor from the cosine/sine pair: their squared evaluation coefficients sum to one for each frequency. The same estimate proves uniform absolute convergence of this odd Fourier series. Hence

    delta^2<=S<=2eta/pi.                              (2)

This proves the first claimed inequality, including polygons.

## 3. Mean-square opposite-support-point sum

For almost every angle the support point `x(theta)` is unique and

    x(theta)=h(theta)u(theta)+h'(theta)u_perp(theta),

where `u=(cos theta,sin theta)` and `u_perp=(-sin theta,cos theta)`. Nondifferentiability of the Lipschitz support function occurs only on a null set, and at every differentiability direction the support face is a singleton. The formula is therefore enough for the integral in the claim; arbitrary choices on the exceptional null set do not affect it.

Since `u(theta+pi)=-u(theta)` and likewise for `u_perp`, removal of the first harmonics gives, almost everywhere,

    x(theta)+x(theta+pi)-2c
      =2(f(theta)u(theta)+f'(theta)u_perp(theta)).

Orthogonality and `H^1` Parseval give

    (1/(2pi))integral_0^{2pi}|x(theta)+x(theta+pi)-2c|^2 dtheta
      =2sum_{j>=3, j odd}(1+j^2)(a_j^2+b_j^2).

For `j>=3`, `(1+j^2)/(j^2-1)<=10/8=5/4`. Together with (1), this proves

    mean-square opposite-support-point sum error
      <=(5/2)S<=5eta/pi.                              (3)

This is a correspondence between opposite NORMAL directions, not a permutation or involution of any supplied finite point labels.

## 4. Sharp constant-width example

Take `h(theta)=R+eps cos(3theta)` with `0<eps<R/8`. Its curvature radius is

    h+h''=R-8eps cos(3theta)>0,

so it defines a smooth strictly convex body. Its width is identically `2R=D`; since the diameter of a convex body is the maximum of its widths, its actual diameter is `D`. Moreover

    x(theta)-x(theta+pi)=D u(theta),

so every boundary support point has an opposite support point at distance exactly `D`.

The Steiner point is zero and the exact quantities are

    eta=4pi eps^2,
    delta=2eps,
    |x(theta)+x(theta+pi)|^2
      =4eps^2(cos^2(3theta)+9sin^2(3theta)).

The last expression has average `20eps^2=5eta/pi` and maximum `36eps^2`. Thus the maximum individual sum error is `6eps`, and the coefficient `5/pi` in (3) is attained exactly.

The center zero also minimizes the Hausdorff reflection defect among all possible centers: in the three directions `0,2pi/3,4pi/3`, the residual odd support value after a translation by `z` is `eps-z dot u`. Their average is `eps`, since the three unit vectors sum to zero. At least one residual is at least `eps`, so no translation makes the defect smaller than `2eps`.

For fixed `t>0`, choosing `eps=t sqrt(D)` is admissible once `D>(16t)^2`. It gives exactly `eta=4pi t^2 D` and `delta=2t sqrt(D)`. This verifies the claimed coarse geometric obstruction; it is not a finite packing or unit-edged polygon example.

## 5. Regular odd unit rim: exact constants

Let `N>=5` be odd, `a=pi/(2N)`, and `K_N` the regular unit-side `N`-gon with circumradius `R_N`. Then

    R_N=1/[2sin(2a)],
    D_N=2R_N cos(a)=1/[2sin(a)],
    A_N=(N/4)cot(2a).

Thus

    eta_N=pi/[16sin^2(a)]-(N/4)cot(2a).

Using `N=pi/(2a)`, `csc^2(a)=a^(-2)+1/3+O(a^2)`, and `cot(2a)=(2a)^(-1)-2a/3+O(a^3)`, one obtains

    eta_N=5pi/48+O(N^(-2)).                           (4)

The constant is `pi/48+pi/12=5pi/48`; no factor of two is missing.

Because `N` is odd, reflection rotates the regular polygon by `pi/N=2a` modulo its rotational symmetries. On a fundamental angular interval `0<=theta<=2a`, the two support functions differ by

    R_N[cos(theta)-cos(2a-theta)].

This decreases from `R_N(1-cos(2a))` to its negative. Therefore

    d_H(K_N,-K_N)=R_N(1-cos(2a))=(1/2)tan(a).         (5)

In particular `D_N d_H=1/[4cos(a)]`, tending to `1/4`.

For a fixed vertex `v`, the two labels nearest `-v` differ from its angular direction by `2a`. Their vector-sum length is

    min_{w in V_N}|v+w|=2R_N sin(a)=1/[2cos(a)].       (6)

Every actual diameter edge also has this sum magnitude. Equations (4)--(6) verify all requested regular-rim constants.

The claimed positive physical stress checks independently: the full unit graph is the boundary cycle, the full diameter graph is the step-`(N-1)/2` cycle, and assigning `mu=D_N^2/N`, `lambda=1/N` gives equilibrium because

    D_N^2[2-2cos(2pi/N)]=2+2cos(pi/N).

Both normalizations and positivity follow directly.

## 6. Wording correction: nearest labels, bijections, and involutions

Equation (6) is a nearest-label statement about reflection through zero. It must not be described as the value of the previously defined involution defect

    min_{iota,c}max_i|p_i+p_{iota(i)}-2c|.

An arbitrary bijection CAN achieve (6): the cyclic shift `j -> j+(N-1)/2 mod N` sends every vertex to a nearest reflected label. Its inverse is the other nearest shift. Neither shift is an involution for odd `N>=5`. Thus a global bijective matching happens to exist here, but that fact needs this explicit construction rather than an inference from separate per-vertex minima.

Every admissible involution on odd `N` has a fixed label `k`. In fact its defect, with ANY choice of center `c`, is at least `R_N`. To see this, denote the maximum residual by `e`. The fixed label gives `e>=2|p_k-c|`. Since the regular vertices sum to zero and an involution permutes the labels, averaging all residual VECTORS gives `-2c`; hence `e>=2|c|`. The triangle inequality then gives

    R_N=|p_k|<=|p_k-c|+|c|<=e.

Thus the odd rim's actual all-label involution defect is at least of order `D_N`, even though the center-zero per-vertex nearest-reflected-label error in (6) tends to `1/2` and the hull Hausdorff error in (5) tends to zero. The claimed discrete obstruction is valid, but these three quantities must be kept distinct.

## Scope and attribution

Worker414 supplied the Fourier inequalities and examples; this audit independently checks the constants and the nonsmooth passage, and makes the label-correspondence qualification explicit. The support/Steiner identities and Reinhardt rim construction are classical. The original worker's primary pointers are DOI `10.1007/s00022-025-00783-4` for the support-function identities and DOI `10.1007/s10107-025-02244-x` for Reinhardt background. No new historical priority, general discrete rigidity, or Erdos99 resolution is claimed.

# Audit: exact irrational unit-lattice loaded endpoints

## Verdict and scope

The arithmetic statement is correct. Let P be a finite planar set of positive diameter D, and let G+ be any nonempty collection of actual diameter pairs. Suppose all their endpoints S lie in one translate

L = p0 + Z u + Z v,   |u| = |v| = 1,

with c = u dot v irrational. Then G+ has at most two edges and |S| <= 4. Only S, not all of P, must lie in L.

Consequently, using the previously checked ORIGINAL-POINT joint-maximal-support endpoint bound, a triangle-free ordinary local diameter minimum with D >= 9 cannot have all loaded endpoints of its joint-maximal physical stress in such a lattice. The passage from the selected representative back to the original support is explained below; preservation of lattice coordinates during selection is neither assumed nor needed.

This audit makes no approximation, near-lattice, or literature-priority claim.

## 1. Equal norms separate the two integer invariants

Irrationality of c excludes c = +/-1, so u and v are linearly independent. Every displacement between points of S has a unique integer coordinate pair (a,b), and

|a u + b v|^2 = a^2 + b^2 + 2c ab.

Choose one diameter displacement with coordinates (a0,b0). Any other diameter displacement (a,b) satisfies

[a^2+b^2-a0^2-b0^2] + 2c[ab-a0b0] = 0.

Both bracketed quantities are integers. Since c is irrational, both vanish. Thus

A = a^2+b^2 = a0^2+b0^2,
B = ab = a0b0

are fixed integers for every such displacement.

Now

(a+b)^2 = A+2B = (a0+b0)^2,
(a-b)^2 = A-2B = (a0-b0)^2.

Independent choices of the two signs yield only

(a,b) in { (a0,b0), (-a0,-b0), (b0,a0), (-b0,-a0) }.

Therefore there are at most four oriented diameter vectors, or at most two unoriented diameter directions.

This includes the degeneracies a0=0 or b0=0. If a0=b0 or a0=-b0, some listed solutions coincide, reducing the count. The zero pair cannot occur because D>0. Signs of B cause no additional solutions.

## 2. A diameter direction supports only one diameter edge

This geometric fact does not require a lattice or unit separation.

Suppose two diameter edges are parallel. Orient them consistently and write them as

{x,x+w},   {y,y+w},   |w|=D.

Put delta=y-x. Because all four endpoints belong to a diameter-D set,

|delta+w| <= D,   |delta-w| <= D.

The parallelogram identity gives

2|delta|^2+2D^2
  = |delta+w|^2+|delta-w|^2
  <= 2D^2.

Hence delta=0, and the two unordered edges are identical. The argument also covers shared endpoints; a cross-distance of zero is harmless.

There is therefore at most one actual diameter edge in each unoriented direction. Applying Section 1 to G+ gives

|G+| <= 2,   |S| <= 2|G+| <= 4.

Actual diameter pairs with endpoints outside S are not counted by this arithmetic argument.

## 3. Why the original joint-MAX support quantifiers suffice

The relevant checked dependency is the original-point statement in Section 5 of outputs/erdos99-cyclic-core-normal-form.md, not merely the selected-representative statement.

Let P be the original triangle-free ordinary local minimum, and let G+(P), S(P) come from a JOINT maximal-support normalized physical certificate. Here joint maximal support covers the union of positive contact AND positive diameter coordinates over all physical certificates.

The accepted finite weak-row release supplies an arbitrarily nearby feasible point R at fixed upper diameter D that strictly shortens every actual diameter pair omitted from G+(P). Choose it inside an open local-minimum neighborhood of P, with no new contacts. Local minimality forces its diameter to remain D, and

E_D(R) is a subset of G+(P).

R is itself an ordinary local minimum: it lies inside the original open neighborhood on which every feasible configuration has diameter at least D.

Next choose a sufficiently small OPEN neighborhood of R in which every noncontact and every nondiametral pair at R retains its strict slack. Perform the checked local lexicographic contact-count/diameter-pair normalization there, obtaining Q. Its actual diameter pairs satisfy

E_D(Q) subset E_D(R) subset G+(P).

Consequently, as sets of point LABELS,

H(Q) subset S(P).

The selected endpoint count gives

2|H(Q)| >= ceil(D)+2.

Thus

2|S(P)| >= ceil(D)+2,

and D>=9 implies |S(P)|>=6. This contradicts the exact lattice bound |S(P)|<=4.

Coordinates of these labels may move off the original lattice during release or normalization. The proof transfers only their cardinality; it never applies lattice arithmetic to Q.

Without the original-point release/subset argument, a selected-only endpoint theorem would not justify this conclusion. An arbitrary nonmaximal certificate, or maximality only over contact coordinates, is not the support hypothesis used here.

## 4. Rational and approximate cases

For a square lattice, c=0 is rational. Equal norms then need only fix a^2+b^2, and need not fix ab. Such examples do not contradict this theorem.

The proof uses exact membership in one lattice and exact equality of diameter lengths. It supplies no stability estimate for points merely close to a lattice, and it imposes no lattice condition on the remaining packing points or on the contact network.

## Final checked conclusion

Under the accepted original-point joint-maximal-support normal form, no triangle-free ordinary local diameter minimum with D>=9 has all its positively loaded diameter endpoints in a single equal-length-basis lattice with irrational basis cosine. The exact endpoint arithmetic itself applies to any finite diameter set and any specified collection of its diameter pairs.

# Audit: linear diameter-degree excess from rhombus tracks

**Verdict: PASS under the supplied selected-core normal form, including the additional fact that EVERY convex-hull vertex is an actual-diameter endpoint.** The hull-visit subsequence can be chosen as proposed. The mixed-track/bridge and nonquadrilateral charges are disjoint within their respective budgets. The proof gives the slightly stronger intermediate bound

    h <= 4+5 delta+3q,

and therefore

    h <= 4+5 eta,  where eta=2k-h.

This note verifies Root's proposal, rather than importing a statement about arbitrary plane contact graphs. It uses the full selected-core hypotheses set out next. No conclusion about all global optimizers or all point labels beyond the existing normal form is asserted.

## 1. Hypotheses and notation

Let `G` be the straight FULL contact graph of the selected connected, nontrivial, triangle-free positive core. Its edges have unit length; every such edge has positive contact weight, and every actual diameter edge has positive diameter weight. Let `h` be the number of actual-diameter endpoint vertices, `k` the number of actual diameter edges, and `b` the number of edge TRAVERSALS in the outer facial walk, counting a bridge twice. Assume the supplied normal form:

* Actual diameter endpoints are strictly exposed convex-hull vertices.
* Every bounded face has a Jordan boundary.
* Every unit quadrilateral face is a convex rhombus whose acute axis angle is strictly greater than 60 degrees.
* With `delta=sum_{bounded faces}(length-4)`, one has `delta>=0` and `b+delta<=2k`.

All convex-hull vertices are indeed among these `h` endpoints. If a hull vertex had zero diameter load, its positive contact equilibrium would express it as a positive weighted average of its unit neighbors, contradicting extremality. Each core vertex has a positive unit incidence because the core is connected and nontrivial. Thus the convex hull has EXACTLY these `h` corners. Collinear noncorner vertices on a hull side do not create exceptions.

Put `q=b-h` and `eta=2k-h`. Then

    q>=0,  q+delta<=eta.                             (1)

For `h<=4`, the desired conclusion follows immediately from `eta>=0`. Hence below assume `h>=5`; the hull is two-dimensional and `b>2`.

## 2. Convex-order visits in the outer walk

**Outer-visit lemma.** In a connected finite plane straight graph, one can choose one outer facial-walk visit at each strictly exposed hull vertex so that the chosen visits occur in their convex cyclic order.

To justify the lemma, take a sufficiently small regular closed neighborhood of the embedded graph. Its outer boundary is a Jordan curve, and traversing it retracts to the outer facial walk, with separate boundary passages corresponding to repeated visits at cutvertices or bridge endpoints. Such a neighborhood can be obtained by sufficiently thin edge strips and vertex disks, or by a sufficiently small generic Euclidean offset. Finiteness and the positive separation between nonincident graph features allow it to be chosen without unintended identifications.

At a hull vertex `s`, select a unit normal strictly exposing `s`. The outer boundary has a point near `s` exposed in this direction, lying on the outer vertex passage that faces away from the hull. For the Euclidean offset it is exactly `s+epsilon n`; choose the normal in the interior of its hull normal cone, so this is on a vertex cap rather than a cap/strip transition. The support directions of the hull vertices have their convex cyclic order. The resulting exposed boundary points occur in that same order on the Jordan curve: otherwise two disjoint curve subarcs would join alternating exposed points of its convex hull, impossible by the Jordan crosscut property. Retracting the passages therefore selects the asserted ordered visits. No claim that a cutvertex has only one outer visit is made.

Choose these `h` visit positions among the `b` cyclic positions of the outer walk. There are `q` unchosen positions. Call an edge traversal good when BOTH its endpoint visit positions are chosen, and bad otherwise. If `g` is the number of good traversals and `z` the number of bad ones, then

    z<=2q,  g=b-z>=b-2q=h-q.                        (2)

The first inequality counts at most the incoming and outgoing traversal at each unchosen position; overlaps only improve it.

Every good traversal joins consecutive chosen hull vertices in convex order. Its edge is consequently a unit SIDE of the convex hull. This identification uses the fact proved in Section 1 that there are no omitted hull corners. Since its length is one, its relative interior contains no further packing vertex.

## 3. Quad tracks are simple paths

Make tracks by continuing through opposite edges of unit quadrilateral faces. A track keeps one fixed unoriented unit-edge axis. Across a rhombus, the segment joining the midpoints of its opposite edges is strictly monotone in a normal coordinate to that axis. When the track passes through their shared edge into the next quadrilateral, that next face lies on the other side of the edge, so the same direction of normal monotonicity continues. Thus tracks have no cycles and no self-intersections. They terminate at an edge incidence whose other side is either the outer face or a nonquadrilateral bounded face.

Equivalently, form an auxiliary graph whose vertices are contact edges incident to a quadrilateral, with adjacency for opposite edges of a quadrilateral. Every auxiliary degree is at most two; normal monotonicity excludes cycle components, so its components are paths. This formulation also proves uniqueness of the track using any endpoint edge incidence. Edges incident to no quadrilateral are handled separately below.

## 4. At most four good ends on good-to-good tracks

A track with two good outer ends joins two parallel unit sides of the convex hull. They must be the two opposite supporting sides for that axis. Its interior lies in the interior of the convex hull: midpoint segments inside quadrilateral faces lie in their interiors, and an intermediate edge on the hull boundary could not have quadrilaterals on both sides. Hence it is a simple crosscut between those supporting sides.

Take two such tracks with different axes. Their four endpoint sides alternate around the convex hull, because the corresponding outward normals have cyclic order `n,m,-n,-m`. The two crosscuts must meet. Different-axis tracks can meet only inside a common quadrilateral: their interiors otherwise lie in disjoint face interiors, and a shared edge midpoint would force the same axis. At their crossing quadrilateral, their acute axis angle is therefore strictly greater than 60 degrees.

There can be at most two unoriented axes pairwise separated by an acute angle strictly greater than 60 degrees. Three axes would give three successive gaps on the projective direction circle of circumference 180 degrees, each greater than 60 degrees, an impossibility. For a fixed axis a convex polygon has at most two supporting sides parallel to it, and hence at most two good hull-side endpoints. Therefore the TOTAL good-end count on good-to-good tracks is at most four.

Strictness of the 60-degree hypothesis is material; allowing exactly 60 would admit three axes.

## 5. Exhaustive charging of all other good traversals

A nonbridge good outer edge has precisely one bounded face on its other side.

* If that face is a quadrilateral, the good edge is a track endpoint. Unless this is already a good-to-good track, its other end is either a bad outer edge or a nonquadrilateral-face incidence. Charge the good edge to that OTHER endpoint.
* If that bounded face is nonquadrilateral, the good edge is incident to no quadrilateral. Charge it to its own incidence with that bounded face.
* If the good edge is a bridge, charge it to its reverse outer traversal.

These cases exhaust all good traversals. The capacities and disjointness are as follows.

**Bad outer traversals.** An outer edge incident to a quadrilateral is the endpoint of exactly one track; it can receive only one mixed-track charge. A bridge is incident to no quadrilateral, so its reverse-traversal charge cannot coincide with such a track-end charge. The reverse of a good bridge traversal is bad: if both directions were good, uniqueness of each selected endpoint visit would force the two traversals to be consecutive in both cyclic directions, implying `b=2`, already excluded. Distinct good bridges have distinct reverse traversals. Consequently the combined mixed-track and bridge charges use at most `z<=2q` bad outer traversals.

**Nonquadrilateral incidences.** A track-end charge uses an incidence whose other side is a quadrilateral. A direct good-edge charge uses an incidence whose other side is the outer face and is incident to no quadrilateral. Thus these two types are disjoint, and each individual incidence receives at most one charge. Since bounded faces are Jordan, nonquadrilateral face lengths are integers `ell>=5`. Their TOTAL incidence capacity is

    sum_badface ell <=5 sum_badface(ell-4)=5 delta.   (3)

This joint count is important: one must not separately allocate the whole `5 delta` budget to each charge type.

Combining Section 4 with these two capacities gives

    g<=4+5 delta+z<=4+5 delta+2q.                    (4)

## 6. Conclusion

Equations (2) and (4) give
